author: blu
body: The x86-64 instruction selector for the flat LIR (the ratchet step of the LIR design). This is the first codegen-changing step of the middle-end campaign -- where the LIR the `IR/Lir.codex` chapter lowers and allocates finally becomes machine code rather than an opt-in dump. It runs behind a per-function dispatch: a function whose body lies entirely within a construct whitelist is lowered tree -> LIR -> allocated -> x86 here, and everything else falls back to the existing recursive tree emitter (`emit-function-standard` / `emit-function-minimal`), byte-for-byte unchanged.

author: blu
body: **This increment covers straight-line arithmetic, branches, spills, constructor-pattern matches, and direct calls:** integer literals, parameters, `let`, add/subtract/multiply, `if` / `match` (literal, variable, wildcard, or, and constructor patterns), spills, and calls to plain user functions (`LiCall`) -- placing arguments in the argument registers, keeping the heap-collision stack guard for a non-leaf, and leaving self-tail- recursive functions on the tree path where TCO turns them into loops. A value live across a call is safe because the allocator only uses callee-saved registers, which the callee preserves. A spilled operand is loaded from its slot into a scratch before use; a spilled destination is computed in a scratch and stored back; a spilled parameter is stored from its argument register into its slot at entry. A constructor pattern loads the variant tag and each bound field from the scrutinee pointer (`LiLoad`). The selector now handles every LIR instruction the lowering emits, so what falls back is exactly what the lowering itself declines: calls, vector patterns, real guards, act blocks, closures, and everything else -- plus, here, functions with more than six parameters (a seventh arrives on the caller's stack, not in a register). The whitelist grows one construct per CL.

author: blu
body: The two moves that bracket this both tend to vanish. The remainder's vreg is hinted to RDX, so taking it out is `mov rdx, rdx`; and where the dividend is already in RAX, putting it there is `mov rax, rax`.

author: blu
body: `nused` and `frame` ride along because a `LiRet` returns from the middle of the layout and has to account for them. `epi` is the block id the shared epilogue is laid out at -- one past the real blocks, so it can be a branch target like any other and be patched by the same machinery.

author: blu
body: Three cuts, and each one was wrong in a way the next made visible. The first ignored `nrets` and asked only whether the epilogue was longer than a jump: it bought fib three instructions and quietly charged one each to ack, locals and tak, every one a single-return function, and the total came out exactly where it started. The second charged a jump at every return including the one that falls through, which reads as a tie at two returns and a two-instruction epilogue and duplicates instead -- `regright` is that shape and it cost an instruction against the tree emitter. The third assumed the fall-through it had just started pricing, and at that same cell with a back-edge laid out last it shares on a tie and pays two five-byte jumps and an epilogue where two two-byte epilogues would do.

author: blu
body: **No benchmark can show that last one and none ever will.** At `(2,2)` the two costs are exactly equal in instructions -- `nrets*e >= nrets+e` for `nrets,e >= 2`, with equality only there -- so the only witness is bytes and executed jumps. It survived two rounds of measurement for that reason. The `epishare` bench is the shape; the harness reports bytes beside instructions because instructions cannot see it.

author: blu
body: Whether the layout ends in a return: the last block that emits anything, since blocks that emit nothing are not where control comes to rest.

author: blu
body: One instruction inside a block. Value instructions (binary, move) and the compare only advance the state; the terminators (branch, jump) also record fixups. A load never reaches a selected block (the dispatch predicate rejects any block containing one), so its case is a defensive no-op.

author: blu
body: A return from where it stands: the value into RAX, the frame released, the callee-saved registers restored, `ret`. It is the same sequence the single exit emits, and an `if` in tail position simply has one per arm instead of driving every arm's value into a shared vreg to hand to one at the end.

author: blu
body: A block records its start offset (by id) before its instructions. Because every control transfer is an explicit branch patched afterwards, the offset table is the only thing layout order feeds into.

author: blu
body: Both sides of the elision must speak this language or neither does. The first cut of the fall-through canonicalised only what the layout falls INTO and left the jump's own target raw, so an arm ending `LiJump exit` compared the exit block's id against the epilogue's and missed: `let v = if c then a else b in v` seals an empty exit that both arms jump to, and each of them emitted `E9 00 00 00 00` -- five bytes of jump to the instruction underneath. Every benchmark returns from its arms, so not one of them has a non-tail join exit and not one of them noticed.

author: blu
body: **This is a parallel move, and the reason is a lesson.** It used to be a sequence, one move per parameter in parameter order, on the stated grounds that every destination was a callee-saved register or a stack slot and so disjoint from the argument registers. That was true the day it was written. Then the leaf register file put `RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX` into `lir-phys` at `5..8`, so that a leaf could keep its parameters in the registers they arrived in -- and from that moment a destination could be *another parameter's arrival register*. The comment kept vouching for an invariant the code had lost, and nothing re-checked it.

author: blu
body: What it cost: `col-hue` in the foreword's Color chapter takes five parameters and divides. The division masks RDX out of the free set for every value live across it, so parameter 2 cannot keep the register it arrived in and is placed in RCX -- which is where parameter 3 arrives. In order, that emits `mov rcx,rdx` and then `mov rbx,rcx`, and the second move reads a register the first one has already overwritten: `mx` is handed `b`. `col-hue` answers 60 where it should answer 0, `rgb-to-hsl` reports red as yellow, and the whole thing was invisible to every gate the campaign had -- the benchmarks measure speed and this is an answer, the fixed point proves determinism and a deterministic wrong answer is still a fixed point, and the allocation verifier never sees these moves at all because they are emitted before the blocks and are not LIR instructions.

author: blu
body: It halts rather than warns. A warning here is a warning that the binary about to be written computes something other than the program, which is not a thing a build should survive; `IR/IRCheck.codex` reaches the same conclusion about malformed IR for the same reason.

author: blu
body: The epilogue is laid out after every block, at the id the returns branch to. A function with a single exit falls into it with its result operand, exactly as before. A function whose every path returns emits it once if it is worth sharing, and not at all if each return already carried its own.
